newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Social Democrats softer to far right.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Social Democrats softer to far right.

text.p: Austria's ruling Social Democrats moved tentatively to embrace the far right on Monday when a senior politician came out in favour of abandoning the strategy of isolating Joerg Haider's Freedom Party.

Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl, the most influential Social Democrat after the chancellor, urged his party to open a dialogue with the Freedom Party after a decade of failed exclusion tactics accompanied by a surge in the far-right vote.
"Haider has drawn his strength from his so-called isolation," Haeupl told Austrian radio.
In two magazine interviews published on Monday, the Vienna mayor called on new chancellor and Social Democratic party leader Viktor Klima to be flexible in his search for a parliamentary majority.

"Parliamentary work should be based on the principle of expediency. Viktor Klima has the right to push through the policies he believes in, regardless of where he draws majority support," he told Germany's Spiegel magazine.

The Social Democrats launched a strategy of non-cooperation with the far right in 1986 when Franz Vranitzky took over as party leader and chancellor and Joerg Haider completed his meteoric rise through the Freedom Party ranks.
Vranitzky's decision marked the beginning of the "grand coalition" of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party that has dominated Austrian politics for the past decade.

In that time support for the Social Democrats has slumped to a post-World War Two low and the far right has managed to triple its share of the vote, mounting a serious challenge to the coalition partners.
Earlier this month, announcing his resignation from politics, Vranitzky conceded that with hindsight he may have underestimated Haider.

Vranitzky's successor Viktor Klima is a pragmatist who has kept his political options open. On Monday he ruled out a coalition with Haider's party but neatly sidestepped questions about possible cooperation.
"A coalition with Haider's Freedom Party is out of the question for the Social Democrats under Klima just as it was out of the question under Vranitzky," Klima told a news conference.
The Freedom Party responded to Haeupl's comments with cautious optimism. Secretary-general Peter Westenthaler spoke of "an interesting thought that opened new possibilities in domestic politics."

Junior coalition partner the People's Party, long considered the most likely candidate for a partnership with the Freedom Party, remained silent. The two parties voted together at the end of last year in an effort to block the sale of bank Creditanstalt to rival Bank Austria.
